1.pericope_label: Joab perceives the king’s mind and suborns the wise woman of Tekoah

schools.summary: Henry takes the warmer sense of the disputed phrase, that the heat of David’s displeasure was over and his old affection survived, so that he wanted only a friend to court him to a reconciliation which would not impeach his justice. He counts four motives in Joab: the courtier studying to ingratiate himself by anticipating what his prince already wished; the friend who had a kindness for Absalom or at least looked on him as the rising sun; the statesman who knew Absalom was the people’s darling and feared a civil war should David die while his son was in exile; and the delinquent, conscious of Abner’s blood and aware that mercy shown to Absalom would help secure his own reprieve. He notes that the parable was laid before the king as Nathan’s had been, so that judgment might be given before the application appeared, and that a mourning widow was sure of a hearing from a king who had himself called God the judge of the widows.

Gill observes that the scene was deliberately laid at a distance so the matter could not easily be inquired into, and canvasses the site of Tekoah, Kimchi putting it in Asher and others in Benjamin while Gill judges it in Judah, with Jerome giving twelve miles from Jerusalem in one place and nine in another. He notes that Amos was of that place and that some have supposed the woman his grandmother, identifies Joab simply as the general of David’s army, and has her come to the palace in the condition and circumstances Joab had prescribed.

Ellicott sets out the crux of the opening phrase, that the Hebrew may mean David’s heart yearned for Absalom, as the versions take it, or that it was hostile to him; the particle is commoner in the latter sense and is unquestionably hostile in the only other place where this form occurs, so he renders it against Absalom and observes that otherwise the stratagem would have been unnecessary. He places Tekoah on a high hill five miles south of Bethlehem, the home of Amos and the birthplace of one of David’s thirty, and near enough to Joab’s own town for him to have known this woman personally; he finds no ground for suspecting her of being a witch or in any way disreputable, and judges the parable Joab’s contrivance but one requiring skill and address in the telling, purposely not made too closely parallel to Absalom’s case lest it defeat its own object. Keil and Delitzsch read the phrase the same way, note that David had not repealed the banishment even after he was comforted for Amnon’s death, and give the calculation behind Joab’s intervention: personal attachment in part, but principally that Absalom had the best prospect of the throne and that this was the surest way to escape punishment for his own murder — hopes which the issue frustrated entirely, since Absalom never succeeded, Joab did not escape, and David was severely chastised for his weakness and injustice.

Clarke enumerates six things built into the disguise which together account for its success: she was a widow, and so her condition of life was calculated to excite compassion; she lived at a distance, which made the case hard to inquire into and the detection unlikely; she was advanced in years, which Josephus thought gave her application more weight; she put on mourning to heighten the idea of distress; she framed a case resembling the king’s own, to convince him that sparing Absalom was reasonable; and she did not make the similitude too plain, lest he see her intention before granting the pardon. He places Tekoah twelve miles from Jerusalem after Jerome. Wesley takes the warmer sense of the opening phrase and explains the paralysis behind it, that the king desired to see his son but was ashamed to show kindness to one whom God’s law and his own conscience obliged him to punish, and therefore wanted a fair pretence, which Joab supplied; on the mourner’s dress he notes only that anointing was what they left off in a mourning state.

debates.question: Was the king’s heart toward Absalom or against him?

positions.view: Against him; the particle is commoner in that sense and is hostile in the only parallel, and on any other reading the stratagem was needless
Toward him; his displeasure had cooled and his old affection survived, wanting only a pretext
In Judah, twelve miles from Jerusalem after Jerome, though he elsewhere says nine
On a high hill five miles south of Bethlehem, near enough to Joab’s town for personal acquaintance
In Asher

outliers.claim: Alone in defending the woman’s character, finding no ground for the suspicion that she was a witch or otherwise disreputable.

themes: a king’s mind read by his general
a preposition that decides the plot
a parable laid at a distance

4.pericope_label: The parable of the two sons, and the oath the widow draws from the king

schools.summary: Henry sets out the motive she imputes to the kinsmen, that they demand the survivor not from any affection to justice or to the memory of the brother they lost but because by destroying the heir the inheritance becomes theirs, which they have the impudence to avow; and he counts the king’s four successive concessions — that he will consider and give order, rather than let the law take its course; that she offered to bear the blame, though Henry cautions that her willingness would not acquit a judge who sentenced without due cognizance; that he promised protection from molestation, which prompts the principle that magistrates ought to be the patrons of oppressed widows; and that he pardoned the son with an oath. In the plea to remember the Lord he hears an appeal to consider how gracious God is, who spared Cain and forgave David the blood of Uriah, and he applies the promise that not a hair shall fall to those under the protection of the Son of David. He doubts whether David did well to shield a man the cities of refuge would not have sheltered, but allows that as the case was presented there was room for mercy to rejoice against judgment, the killing being on a sudden provocation and perhaps in self-defence.

Gill calls the story a fable outright and says she pressed for immediate sentence because it would not bear an inquisition, noting that she spoke with vehemence yet great respect. He observes that two sons are specified so that her case might suit Amnon and Absalom, that not the avenger of blood alone but the whole kindred rose as one man, and that the king’s question asked in effect what her case and circumstances were, intimating readiness to help. On the plea to remember the Lord he reports that some understand her to seek not merely a word but an oath, since to make mention of God is what men do when they swear by him.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the pretended calamity without pronouncing on its truth and work instead on the language, explaining the doubled object in the clause about the brother’s death from the diffuseness of ordinary conversation and refusing the proposed emendation on the ground that the unusual suffix has parallels while the plural would be quite unsuitable; they judge the king’s first answer perfectly just, since a man who killed his brother in the heat of a quarrel ought to be defended from the avenger of blood, and they call the woman crafty for repeating her petition in order to bind him by oath. Ellicott notices what the invention is careful to do, presenting the killing as unpremeditated and without malice, which makes the case essentially unlike Absalom’s, though the object at this stage is only to dispose the king favourably and by the time the application comes the distinction will have passed out of mind; he observes that she puts the threat against the heir into the family’s mouth because that would be the effect of what they ask, with a covert allusion to Absalom as David’s heir certainly intended, and reads her offer to bear the iniquity as a device for prolonging the interview until the king has committed himself more completely.

Clarke stands alone in allowing that the principal facts may have been real and that Joab found a woman whose circumstances already resembled what he wished represented. He works the metaphor of the quenched coal, a man and his descendants being often called a lamp or a light in Scripture, so that to quench the coal is to destroy all hope of posterity and extinguish a family from among the people, and he adds that the heathen used the same figure, the few survivors of the deluge being called living coals because by them the vital flame of the race was to be rekindled. He traces the woman’s advance step by step, each royal concession proving too distant to conclude her business until the oath is given, and reads the plea to remember the Lord as an argument from the divine example, that God grants mercy promptly and does not wait until the case is hopeless. Wesley notes that a widow is one who most needs compassion and whom the law obliges a king in a singular manner to relieve, and reads her offer to bear the iniquity the opposite way from Clarke and Ellicott, as a warning that neglect of her cause would bring guilt upon the king himself, decently phrased so as not to seem to blame or threaten him — a sense he argues agrees best with the answer David gives.

debates.question: Was the widow’s story wholly invented?

positions.view: A fable throughout, which is why she would not risk an inquiry into it
The principal facts may have been real, Joab having found a woman whose case already resembled what he needed

debates.question: What is she doing when she offers to bear the iniquity herself?

positions.view: Assuming the blame for condoning blood-guilt, lest the king think his justice compromised, and prolonging the interview
Warning that neglect of her cause would bring guilt on the king, phrased so as not to seem to threaten him
Offering what would not in fact acquit a judge who sentenced without due cognizance of the case

debates.question: What does the plea to remember the Lord ask for?

positions.view: An oath, since to make mention of God is what men do when they swear
God as witness against the king should he break a promise already made
An argument from the divine example, that God shows mercy promptly and does not wait until the case is hopeless

outliers.claim: Alone in supposing the widow’s case substantially true rather than invented, and alone in illustrating the quenched coal from a heathen parallel.

themes: the heir destroyed for the inheritance

12.pericope_label: The parable applied to Absalom, and Joab’s hand detected behind it

schools.summary: Henry reads the turn as the mask thrown off, the humble petitioner becoming of a sudden the king’s reprover and the mouth of the people, and notes that she never names Absalom because David longed for him too much to mistake whose banishment was meant. He grants that the cases differ materially — Absalom killed not in a sudden passion but on an old grudge, not in the field but at table before his guests, and was no only son — yet observes that David was himself too well affected to the cause to be critical about the disparity. On the king’s detection of Joab he supplies the reason the others lack, that no such woman would have appealed to him in a matter of that moment of her own accord and that he knew none so likely to have set her on as a man at once politic and Absalom’s friend; and he praises her for owning the truth when the scheme had already pleased the king, making her an example that nothing can ever need a lie.

Gill reports from Abarbinel the opinion of Ephodaeus that by the people of God are meant Absalom and his men, or Absalom alone, one man being sometimes called a people, though he prefers the sense that the king’s severity was contrary to the will of Israel, who wished to see Absalom fetched back from a heathen court where he was in danger of corruption. He judges the argument from mortality plausible but bad reasoning in the case of a malefactor, while allowing its force, that David must die and a successor be named and that a disputed succession could prove fatal if Absalom were not recalled in his father’s lifetime. He understands the king to have seen plainly that the case was feigned and framed to convey the mind of the people.

Ellicott holds that by constant usage the people of God can only mean Israel, and traces her method: she must now show the king that his own decision condemns him, so she hints rather than states, first that he wrongs the nation and then that he does so against the spirit of the judgment just given. On the mortality argument he thinks she craftily withdraws attention from the real point, the question of right and justice, assuming what should be proved and urging that delay is unsafe because life is uncertain; and on the disputed clause he holds the English certainly wrong, rendering it that God does not take away the soul but devises thoughts that he may not banish the banished one, the sense being that God in wrath remembers mercy and will not press punishment to extremes. Of the king’s suspicion of Joab he admits he cannot say why it fell there, guessing a courtier’s interest in the heir or, more probably, that Joab had pressed the same request before. Keil and Delitzsch reject the rendering of Dathe and Thenius, who understood the phrase of the protection the king had extended to her own son, on the ground that the construction will not bear it; they note that her words were kept intentionally indefinite, judge her speech so crafty that David could not fail to see both her meaning and that she had not come unprompted, and read her closing flattery as a bid to gain him over completely.

Clarke calls the fourteenth verse very elegant and powerfully persuasive and partly adopts its reasoning, holding that Amnon’s crime was the most flagitious, the injury to Absalom in his sister’s ruin indescribably great, and the king at fault for not administering justice, so that the fratricide, horrible as it is, is a pardonable case. On the disputed clause he agrees the Hebrew says God does not take away the soul, and reports what the versions made of it, the Greek giving that God will receive the soul — which he takes to show that its translators and the Jews of their time already held the soul’s separate existence after death — and the Latin that God does not will the soul’s destruction. He hears in the compliment about an angel’s wisdom the ordinary style of eastern flattery. Wesley spells out the comparison she presses, that if the king will not let two avengers molest her son, it is unreasonable to pursue Absalom, whose death would grieve the whole commonwealth; he reads the clause of no man being exempted from the common law of dying, and takes the people who made her afraid to be the nation, discontented at the perpetual banishment and likely to take up arms if Absalom should invade with his father-in-law’s help.

positions.view: Israel, by constant usage of the phrase
Absalom and his men, or Absalom alone, one man being sometimes called a people
The protection the king had just extended to her own son
held_by: Dathe and Thenius (as reported and rejected by Keil and Delitzsch)

debates.question: Is the argument from mortality a good one?

positions.view: Very elegant and powerfully persuasive, and partly sound, since Amnon’s crime was the greater and the king had failed to do justice
Plausible but bad reasoning in the case of a malefactor
A craft that withdraws attention from the real question of right and justice

That no man is exempted from the common law of dying

an angel’s wisdom, and eastern flattery

21.pericope_label: Absalom fetched from Geshur, but forbidden the king’s face

schools.summary: Henry cannot see how David is to be justified in suspending the ancient law that whoso sheds man’s blood by man shall his blood be shed, and says God’s laws were never designed to be cobwebs which catch the little flies but suffer the great ones to break through; he judges that God justly made the son whom a foolish pity spared into a scourge to his father. He hears in Joab’s thanks what some have taken for an assurance that the murder of Abner would never now be called to account, in which he says Joab was mistaken, as the charge laid on Solomon would show. The interdict he defends on two grounds, the king’s own honour, that he might not seem to countenance so great a criminal or to forgive too easily, and Absalom’s greater humiliation, since something in his conduct when Joab fetched him suggested he was not truly penitent. He alone turns the recall the other way as well, finding in the order to go and bring the young man again an image of the divine method, since God is reconciled to sinners through a Mediator who intercedes and is sent to bring them back.

Gill places Joab close at hand, waiting on the issue of the affair, has him bow to the very ground in reverence, locates Geshur as the place where Absalom had been with his grandfather the king of that country, and understands the order excluding him from the presence to have been given to Joab when the king was told that Absalom had reached Jerusalem.

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew text has the king say that he has done this thing while the margin reads that Joab has done it, the first being simply a form of granting the request and the second conveying an implied censure of the stratagem even while complying with it. On the interdict he separates the two acts by their motives, the return granted in weakness and the exclusion out of a sense of justice, and judges the compound effect unfortunate, since it irritated Absalom while leaving him conveniently placed to carry out his plots; he thinks it probable that Absalom was confined to his own house. Keil and Delitzsch keep the written text here and treat the marginal reading as a misunderstanding, and from Joab’s thanks they infer that he had applied for Absalom’s return repeatedly before without any attention being paid, which is why David suspected his hand behind the woman. They call the half forgiveness an imprudent measure which bore very bitter fruit.

Clarke supposes Joab to have been present throughout the audience, with others of the court besides, and judges the exclusion from the presence highly proper, a way of showing detestation of the crime and respect for justice while remitting the death penalty. Wesley is severe on the recall itself, holding that David had no power to dispense with God’s laws, which bind kings and rulers as much as the people of Israel, and asking how justly God made the man he had so sinfully spared a scourge to him; on the interdict he agrees with Clarke, both lest the king seem to approve the sin and because the exclusion might draw Absalom to a more thorough humiliation and repentance.

debates.question: Was the half-measure — recall without admission to the presence — right?

positions.view: Highly proper, showing detestation of the crime and respect for justice, and apt to bring Absalom to repentance
An imprudent measure which bore very bitter fruit
Unfortunate in its compound effect, irritating Absalom while leaving him placed to plot

debates.question: Does the king say “I have done this thing” or “thou hast done”?

positions.view: The written text, “I have done” — simply the form in which a request is granted
The marginal reading, which would carry an implied censure of Joab’s stratagem
held_by: the Masoretic margin (as reported by Charles Ellicott)

outliers.claim: Alone in reading the order to bring Absalom back as a figure of the divine method of reconciliation through a Mediator’s intercession.

themes: the law suspended for a king’s son
a son in the city and not at court

25.pericope_label: Absalom’s beauty, the weight of his hair, and his children

schools.summary: Henry allows the beauty as fact and nothing more, calling it a poor commendation for a man with nothing else valuable in him, and observing that though his body had no blemish his mind had nothing but wounds and bruises; he suspects the comeliness was one reason his father was so fond of him and shielded him from justice, and warns those who are better pleased with their children’s beauty than their virtue. On the hair he denies the Nazarite reading outright, Absalom being far from that strictness, and makes it the hair of a beau, worn long because pride feels neither cold nor heat, polled only for ostentation and weighed that it might be seen to excel other men’s; he alone defends the received figure, reckoning the weight lower than the moderns do and citing bishop Patrick that with the oil and powder, gold-dust if Josephus is right about the fashion, the number is not at all incredible. He notes that the fine hair proved his halter. On the children he allows that they may have died young, but offers the alternative that they were cut off by the righteous hand of God while he was hatching his rebellion, the pillar following their loss.

Gill says the beauty is recorded to account in some measure for the hold Absalom had on the people’s affections, then and afterwards, and that the good head of hair was part of what made him comely. He infers that the three sons very probably died young, both because their names are not given and because Absalom is elsewhere said to have had no son and to have raised a pillar to keep his name in remembrance, which he thinks unlikely to have been set up before the sons were born.

Keil and Delitzsch read a strong growth of hair as a sign of great manly power and so far a proof of Absalom’s beauty, but call the figure of two hundred shekels in any case a round number and much too high, reasoning that the sacred reckoning gives about six pounds and that even if the royal shekel were half the sacred one the number would remain far too great. They take the omission of the sons’ names, contrary to general usage, to mean that they died in infancy, which is why Absalom afterwards erected a pillar, and read the daughter’s name as a proof of his affection for the sister Amnon had violated; the Greek addition that she became the wife of Rehoboam they note is quite at variance with the record that his wife and Abijah’s mother was Maachah, and they report that Thenius defended the clause as original on grounds Böttcher showed to be worthless. Ellicott reaches the same arithmetic from the same unknown value of the royal shekel and concludes that some clerical error has probably arisen in copying the number; he confirms the sons’ early death from Absalom’s own words that he had no son to keep his name in remembrance, notes that the daughter bore her aunt’s name and shared her beauty, and alone rescues the substance of the Greek gloss by reconstruction: Maachah is called Absalom’s daughter yet Abijah is elsewhere called the son of Michaiah the daughter of Uriel, so Maachah must be Absalom’s granddaughter — Tamar married Uriel, and her daughter became the mother of a line of kings.

Clarke says it was probably the personal beauty that made the public interest itself in Absalom, the mass of men being ever caught and led by outward appearances, and that he was perfect and regular in all his features. On the hair he reviews Bochart’s defence of the received figure from the lavish ancient use of oils and ointments and from Josephus on the Jews putting gold dust in their hair that it might flame in the sun, reports Josephus’s own reckoning of twelve and a half pounds and a head that took eight days to shear, which he dismisses, records the view of some that the word gives the value rather than the weight, and then proposes his own solution, that the letter standing for two hundred was misread for the one standing for thirty, whose upper stroke is easily worn in manuscripts, adding that the phrase rendered at every year’s end means rather at convenient times and that the head was polled, the redundancy cut off, not shaved. On the daughter he reports that the Greek adds she became Rehoboam’s wife and bore him Abia, that Josephus says the same, and that no other version has the addition. Wesley makes the beauty the occasion both of Absalom’s pride and of the people’s affection, records without deciding the view that the weight is really the price of the hair, and agrees that the sons died soon after birth.

The text is corrupt in a specifiable way: thirty was misread as two hundred, the letters being easily confused
The text stands; with oil and powder, and gold dust in the fashion of the time, the weight is not incredible
held_by: bishop Patrick (as reported by Matthew Henry)

positions.view: The number gives the value of the hair, not its weight

debates.question: Did Tamar become the wife of Rehoboam, as the Greek adds?

positions.view: A confused gloss, but its substance is recoverable: Tamar married Uriel, and her daughter Maachah married Rehoboam
Quite at variance with the record elsewhere, and defended as original only on worthless grounds
Reported as the Greek and Josephus give it, with the note that no other version has it

outliers.claim: Alone in defending the received weight of the hair, and alone in denying that it is to be read as a Nazarite’s.

a numeral and a worn letter
a daughter named for her aunt

28.pericope_label: Two years without the king’s face, and the burning of Joab’s barley

schools.summary: Henry holds that after three years abroad and two as a prisoner at large Absalom had been dealt with better than he deserved, yet his spirit was unhumbled and his pride unmortified, and that instead of being thankful his life was spared he reckoned himself wronged not to be restored to court; had he truly repented, the distance from the gaieties of the court and his retirement in the holy city would have been agreeable, and if a murderer must live let him be for ever a recluse. He reads the longing to see the king’s face as pretended love and real ambition, the snake unable to sting again until warmed in his father’s bosom. Joab’s refusal he puts down to Absalom’s never having thanked him properly for the recall, proud men taking every service done them for a debt, and he notes that Samson could think of no greater injury to the Philistines than firing their corn, marvelling that a man should hope to win a kindness by doing a mischief. He alone observes that the law required restitution for the burnt corn and that neither party raised it, and suspects Joab was frightened at such boldness and reckoned Absalom already strong enough among the people to carry him through, which shows what some men accomplish by threats and carrying things with a high hand; against which he sets the one comfortable reading, that God by afflictions brings to himself those who keep at a distance.

Gill counts the two full years from the return out of Geshur, says Absalom was uneasy at being confined to his own house and not suffered to come to court, identifies the servants as those who kept his flocks and tilled his ground, and observes that Joab came provoked and to learn the reason — which was exactly Absalom’s end.

Keil and Delitzsch set out the calculation exactly: Absalom sent twice for Joab to obtain full forgiveness and was twice refused, and so had a field fired which adjoined his own and stood full of barley, foreseeing that Joab would not take the destruction of his property quietly but would come to complain of it; they gloss the phrase for its position as literally at his hand, note the variation between written and marginal forms of the imperative, and repeat their verdict that the half forgiving was really worse than no forgiveness at all. Ellicott accounts for Joab’s refusal differently, supposing he judged he had gone far enough already in procuring the return, that he was himself still under the king’s displeasure and so disinclined to do more, and possibly also that he thought Absalom should have shown some sign of penitence for his great crime; he grants the stratagem was perfectly successful and adds that it would only have been resorted to by a lawless and unscrupulous character.

Clarke calls the conduct strange but notes the irony of its working: Joab, who had not used his influence to bring Absalom to court, now uses it and succeeds. He had not interceded to bring Absalom to court while he was merely asked; the loss of a field moves him at once.

debates.question: Why would Joab not come when Absalom sent for him?

positions.view: He judged he had gone far enough, was still under the king’s displeasure, and may have looked for some sign of penitence
Because Absalom had never thanked him properly for the recall, proud men taking every service for a debt

debates.question: Where does the fault for this impasse lie?

positions.view: In the half forgiveness, which was worse than no forgiveness at all
In Absalom, who was dealt with better than he deserved and remained unhumbled

outliers.claim: Alone in noticing that the law obliged Absalom to make restitution for the burnt corn, and that neither he offered it nor Joab demanded it.

themes: two years in the city, unseen
what men gain by a high hand

32.pericope_label: Absalom’s demand to be killed or pardoned, and the king’s kiss

schools.summary: Henry calls the message haughty and imperious and unbecoming either a son or a subject: it undervalues the favour already shown in the recall from Geshur, denies the crime outright, and defies the king’s justice in words the speaker knows are safe, since he counts on being loved too well for them to be acted upon. He judges that David’s strong affection construed the bowing and the words as the language of a great respect and an earnest desire of his favour when it was far otherwise, and draws the lesson that wise and good men are easily imposed upon by children they are blindly fond of. Yet he will not end on the politics: the father’s bowels prevailed to reconcile him to an impenitent son, and from that he argues to the greater case, that penitent sinners need not question the compassion of the Father of mercies, pressing it with the prophet’s word that when Ephraim bemoans himself God soon bemoans him and calls him a dear son and a pleasant child.

Gill finds no repentance in the answer at all: Absalom neither denies the fact nor is ashamed of it nor asks pardon for it, but sets about vindicating it by giving what he takes to be a sufficient reason. Of the last verse he notes only that Joab carried to the king what Absalom had said to him.

Ellicott grants that Absalom makes no acknowledgment of having done wrong, but gives the demand a logic the others withhold: the state of half-reconciliation is intolerable, and he must either be punished or fully pardoned. Joab’s intercession then accomplishes its purpose, the king receives him and kisses him in token of complete reconciliation, and in this, Ellicott judges, David showed great weakness, for which he afterwards suffered severely. Keil and Delitzsch, having called the earlier half-forgiveness worse than none at all, allow that Absalom might very properly desire to be dealt with according to the law, and let the full reconciliation stand as the sequel their verdict predicted.

Wesley hears flattery rather than either defiance or logic: better to die than to want the sight and favour of a dear father is an insinuation into the affections Absalom means to exploit. He marks the trajectory, that by this time, having so far recovered his father’s favour, Absalom had begun to grow upon him and had gathered confidence enough to stand upon his own justification, as though what he had done were no iniquity, or at least none deserving death; and he draws the same warning as Henry, that wise parents are easily imposed on by children they are blindly fond of, closing with the same turn from the father’s reconciliation of an impenitent son to the compassion of the Father of mercies toward penitent ones.

debates.question: What is Absalom doing when he offers his own life?

positions.view: Defying the king’s justice, knowing he is loved too well for the offer to be taken up
Vindicating the deed without repentance, neither denying it nor asking pardon
Demanding resolution of an intolerable half-state: either punishment or full pardon
Insinuating himself into his father’s affections by a pretence of love

outliers.claim: Alone in granting Absalom’s demand a logic of its own, that a half-reconciliation was intolerable and had to end either in punishment or in full pardon.

themes: wherefore am I come from Geshur
a kiss that sealed a pardon
from a fond father to the Father of mercies
